replying_to: Replying to Feature Shapley: A general framework to discovering useful feature interactions
display_title: Official Review of Paper93 by Reviewer Rc5u

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an interesting approach for improving predictions by focusing on learning interactions over improving a particular algorithm. The paper proposes "Feature Shapley", an approach for explicitly learning important feature interactions using Shapley values.
content.main_review:
Strong points:
- The focus on capturing the correct feature interactions to use is interesting -- many approaches consider feature selection by considering individual features (and not interactions)
- The paper is well-motivated: often, too much attention in prediction problems is paid to incrementally improving an algorithm when a greater focus on the mean model could result in larger improvements
- The comparisons of the proposed approach to other methods are thorough (though only on the original datasets; characterizing these as "experiments" is misleading)

Major concerns:
- My main concern about the paper is the lack of experimentation and reproducibility.
    - Experimentation: a deeper analysis of the proposed method is necessary. Consider generating data under a wide variety of scenarios (with a large and small (or zero) number of interactions, with complex or simple mean models, binary and continuous outcomes, etc.) to fully explore the properties of the method.
    - The example in Section 4.6 is not clearly explained, and the figure is unclear.
    - The experiments and data analyses need to be clearly explained so that they can be reproduced. Code should be made available.
- The proposed approach, while well-motivated and interesting, does not appear novel. Shapley values have been used many times for feature importance, and the literature is full of examples where attention is paid to modeling the correct interactions between features. A clearer motivation for the proposal, and where it sits in the literature, would be good (including less focus on the approach as "novel").  It is possible that Equation (2) is the novel approach, and this could be highlighted (rather than equation 1) and explained.
- The exposition could be improved in many places: for example, what is the interpretation of using the learned features (end of Section 2)? if the goal is beyond prediction, how do we account for the fact that we've used the data twice (once for learning the interactions, and a second time for estimation)?; sections 4.1 and 4.2 could be combined and streamlined; the order of sections 5.2 and 5.1 could be switched and streamlined.
- Why did you focus on linear models? It seems that other methods could provide an even larger performance boost (and you mention this in the conclusion); these methods should be simple to implement and shouldn't add much to computation time (since the bulk of computation time likely comes from estimating the Shapley values)

Minor comments:
- the GitHub link in footnote 2 is incorrect, it should be https://github.com/WeiyuCheng/AFN-AAAI-20
- there are typos throughout
- Figure 2 could be better explained, particularly panel (c)
content.summary_of_the_review: I vote for rejecting the paper. The exposition of the paper needs to be improved (including less emphasis on the method as "novel"), and the experiments need to test the method in a wider array of settings.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

content.title: Response to reviewer 4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive and detailed comments. Please refer to the following for our response:

a)“My main concern about the paper is the lack of experimentation and reproducibility.”

In this work, we verify the effectiveness of our method on two important tasks, CTR prediction and asset pricing. For CTR prediction, we conduct experiments on different sizes of datasets. Specifically, MovieLens is a relatively small dataset, which only include 3 feature fields. Meanwhile, Frappe is a medium size dataset for CTR prediction, and Avazu is a relatively large dataset. Since CTR prediction task aims to generate binary outcomes, we also consider the asset pricing task, whose outputs are continuous.  
We agree with the reviewer that more experiments should be conducted to investigate the properties of our method.  We will conduct more experiments on the asset pricing datasets due to its appropriate number of features. Specifically, we will make a comparison between the accurate Shapley value and our Feature Shapley value. We will also discuss the computational cost of our methods. The datasets and source code will be released upon acceptance.

b) "The proposed approach, while well-motivated and interesting, does not appear novel. Shapley values have been used many times for feature importance, and the literature is full of examples where attention is paid to modeling the correct interactions between features. A clearer motivation for the proposal, and where it sits in the literature, would be good (including less focus on the approach as "novel"). It is possible that Equation (2) is the novel approach, and this could be highlighted (rather than equation 1) and explained."

Thank you for your suggestion. We realized that most of the existing works focus on estimating the contribution of an individual feature to the model performance. In this work, we apply Shapley value to estimate how much an individual feature contribute to a feature interaction. As such, useful feature interactions will be discovered effectively. We will  present the relationships between our method and related works in more detail.

c) "The exposition could be improved in many places: for example, what is the interpretation of using the learned features (end of Section 2)? if the goal is beyond prediction, how do we account for the fact that we've used the data twice (once for learning the interactions, and a second time for estimation)?; sections 4.1 and 4.2 could be combined and streamlined; the order of sections 5.2 and 5.1 could be switched and streamlined."

Thank you for your suggestion. In fact, other methods which aims to explicitly model the feature interaction (e,g, AutoFIS) also takes two stages and used data twice. In our work, we use a linear model to discover useful feature interactions due to its natural interpretability. To further improve the performance of prediction, we show that only a single layer neural network is able to achieve SOTA performance.  We will improve some imprecise expressions  carefully based on your valuable suggestions. 

d) “Why did you focus on linear models? It seems that other methods could provide an even larger performance boost (and you mention this in the conclusion); these methods should be simple to implement and shouldn't add much to computation time (since the bulk of computation time likely comes from estimating the Shapley values)”

We focus on linear model because of the following reasons: 1) Since our method takes more time in the training stage, we hence adopt a linear model to avoiding too much computational cost during the training process. 2)The linear model is naturally interpretable. This motivates us to discover useful feature interactions based on a linear regression model at first. To achieve higher accuracy, one can feed the original feature and the learned feature interactions into a more complex model.

f) “Other Minor comments”

We appreciate the reviewer to point out the typos in this manuscript. We will provide a more detailed description of Figure 2(c) in the updated manuscript.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents an algorithm to estimate feature shapley value with reasonable computational cost. Capturing important feature interaction becomes practical.
This allows a model to include only important feature interactions and simple model with important feature interaction can performance well
Experiment result shows the benefit of this approach
content.main_review:
Strengths:
  1. Clearly presents the importances of feature interactions. It does the heavy lifting to calculate the feature interaction value, filter out unimportant feature interactions, and only include the important interactions in the model. 
Instead, most of the current approach is to use general model techniques to utilize feature interactions, which is computational intensive, requires large memory, and huge search space.
  2. The optimization of the shapely calculation seems reasonable

Weekness:
  1. The experiment dataset may not be big enough to show long term gain
  2. What is the accuracy gap between calculating Shapley value using its definition versus using this algorithm?
  3. It is not unique to use shapley for feature selection. This is another paper talking about using shapley value for feature selection. http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~scohen/ijcai05features.pdf
  4. It is not clear how often to calculate the shapley value and therefore update the features to the model input. And how to decide that update frequency? Any trade-off?
content.summary_of_the_review: The main contribution of this paper is not a framework, but an algorithm.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to reviewer 3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive and detailed comments. Please refer to the following for our response:

a.	“The experiment dataset may not be big enough to show long term gain”

Actually, one of the CTR datasets, Avazu is big enough so that our method may not be able to fully exploit all the useful interactions. In our experimentation, we find that the performance of our method LR (Shapley) increases steadily. However, although we have applied approximation to the computation of Shapley value, the training time on Avazu is still too long. Therefore, we have adjusted the size of the threshold parameter in order to make it more likely to meet the end-of-training condition. Even in this case, LR (Shapley) has learned 32 feature interactions on Avazu dataset and achieved satisfactory performance, while comparing methods modeling hundreds or thousands of feature interactions to achieve similar performance. 
																						
b.	“What is the accuracy gap between calculating Shapley value using its definition versus using this algorithm?”

Thank you for raising this concern. We agree with the reviewer that the comparison between the accurate Shapley value and our Feature Shapley value is important for discovering the property of our method. We will conduct this experiment on asset pricing dataset since calculating accurate Shapley value for medium or large CTR datasets such as Frappe and Avazu is impractical. Meanwhile, small datasets such as MovieLens does not need Monte-Carlo approximation because it has only 3 feature fields.

c.	It is not unique to use shapley for feature selection. This is another paper talking about using shapley value for feature selection.  

Thank you for introducing this paper which selects features based on their feature importance. In contrast, our method aims to “generate” feature interactions rather than “delete” useless individual features. We will include this paper in the updated manuscript. 

d.	It is not clear how often to calculate the shapley value and therefore update the features to the model input. And how to decide that update frequency? Any trade-off?

Thank you for your suggestion. We will try to describe the Algorithm 1 in more detail in the updated manuscript. The update frequency depends on whether the useful feature interaction is discovered. In other words, the model will be updated once useful feature interactions are found.

display_title: Official Review of Paper93 by Reviewer UDoq

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed to find useful feature interactions based on feature Shapley value method. The authors utilized the MC-based approach for fast computation of Shapley values. Experiments are carried out on two real-world problems (CTR prediction and price estimation) with comparison to several baselines.
content.main_review:
Strength
1. The authors study an interesting and important problem for automatic feature interaction discovery.
2. The authors carried out a through experiment on two tasks with comparison to several state-of-art DNN-based approaches.

Weakness
1. Some description of the paper is not very clear. First, which level are the feature interactions defined? It is on field level or feature level. In algorithm 1, the author mentioned feature set and number of features in Table 1. However, based on the results in Section 4.6, seems the interaction is on the field level instead. In would be good for a clarification. Second, it is not very clear how the NN (Shapley) model works. Is it cross + embedding?
2. One main motivation to automatically detect interaction is for efficient inference. The authors should include comparison on (1) the inference time for each of the model and the number of parameters (2) the training time for each model (pure training for baselines and interaction detection + training for a fair comparison for the proposed method).
3. Besides the automatic feature interaction selection methods, the authors should compare to work on explicit feature interaction section method like “Feature Interaction Interpretability: A Case for Explaining Ad-Recommendation Systems via Neural Interaction Detection” or the GDBT_LR schema for feature interaction discovery in “Practical lessons from predicting clicks on ads at facebook”.
4. The experiment on the asset pricing is not very illustrative. It is obvious that adding interaction to a linear model would improve the prediction performance. It would be much useful to compare to other methods to find interactions.
5. The proposed method seem a direct application of Shapley value method for CTR model. The proposed MC computation is not innovative and the description of the early step part is not very clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is a direct application of an existing technical. Also there are a few issues in the writing and the experiments in the paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response to reviewer 2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive and detailed comments. Please refer to the following for our response:

a.	“which level are the feature interactions defined? Second, it is not very clear how the NN (Shapley) model works. Is it cross + embedding?

Thank you for raising this concern. We try to capture the field level feature interactions for the CTR task. As for NN (Shapley), we first obtain the embeddings of original features. Then we employ multiplication based on the “dictionary” of learnt feature interactions and generate embeddings of feature interactions. The above embedding vectors are concatenated and fed into a single-layer neural network for prediction. We will include the above explanation in the updated manuscript.

b.	“One main motivation to automatically detect interaction is for efficient inference. The authors should include comparison on (1) the inference time for each of the model and the number of parameters (2) the training time for each model (pure training for baselines and interaction detection + training for a fair comparison for the proposed method).”

Thank you for your suggestion. We agree with the reviewer and have conducted the above experiments. We will add a table to present the running cost of each model.  

c.	“Besides the automatic feature interaction selection methods, the authors should compare to work on explicit feature interaction section method like “Feature Interaction Interpretability: A Case for Explaining Ad-Recommendation Systems via Neural Interaction Detection” or the GDBT_LR schema for feature interaction discovery in “Practical lessons from predicting clicks on ads at facebook”.

Thank you for the suggestion. Actually, AutoFIS is an “explicit feature interaction method”. The chosen feature interactions are then fed into a deep model such as DeepFM for prediction. We are implementing the GDBT_LR method, and the results will be presented in the updated manuscript. 

d.	The experiment on the asset pricing is not very illustrative. It is obvious that adding interaction to a linear model would improve the prediction performance. It would be much useful to compare to other methods to find interactions.

Thank you for your suggestion, we will add comparing methods on the asset pricing task. For example, neural networkd can be applied to model feature interaction implicitly. Furthermore, we will make a comparison between the accurate Shapley value and the Feature Shapley value.   

e.	“The proposed method seem a direct application of Shapley value method for CTR model. The proposed MC computation is not innovative and the description of the early step part is not very clear.”

In this work, we present how to discover useful feature interactions among input features. Note that the proposed method is very flexible as it can be applied on any task that takes feature as the input of machine learning systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Feature Shapley on both CTR task and asset pricing task in this work. We will clarify the MC computation and early stop part in more detail in the updated manuscript.

replying_to: Replying to Feature Shapley: A general framework to discovering useful feature interactions
display_title: Official Review of Paper93 by Reviewer 6APa

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This manuscript proposes an algorithm that uses Shapley's value for model/feature selection at the training stage.

It then demonstrates its technique in two environments, click-through rate (CTR) and asset pricing.

The paper does not sufficiently clearly explain, in my view, how it differs from earlier uses of Shapley's value for model/feature selection (e.g. Lipovetsky & Conklin, 2001; Sundararajan & Najmi, 2020).
content.main_review:
**Strengths**

Feature/model selection is an important problem; the techniques presented here perform well on the chosen datasets against the chosen comparators.

**Weaknesses**

1. _exposition_: 
    1. the manuscript burns space discussing 'data-centric methods'.  In my view, this is a distraction that adds nothing to the main arguments, while cutting down on the space available to properly substantiate those arguments.  I recommend cutting this material and bolstering the main arguments.
    1. there are minor typos and grammatical errors at a few places.  In most cases, the authors' intent is intelligible, but it would be nice to clear them up.
    1. \citep{} should be used in many of the cases that \cite{} or \citet{} is currently used
    1. no footnotes in abstracts, by historical convention
    1. I'd re-draft the abstract to make it a bit clearer: this will be people's first point of contact with the paper
    1. the figures are too small to read
    1. what's the difference between Ghorbani & Zou's 2019 application of Shapley to "each data sample" and "local Shapley values" (in the sense of Lundberg & Lee)?
    1. I missed how the "toy" MovieLens analysis in \S 4.6 differed from the MovieLens analysis performed earlier in the manuscript.  Thus, I'd recommend clarifying that paragraph.
    1. re: the asset pricing example, I don't know that I'd say it's "_exactly_ a regression task"; in addition to "well-designed" factors, well-learned factors can also be important; I would say that Sharpe's CAPM model is a significant contribution to modern asset pricing theory, not "the birth of asset pricing theory" (Modigliani and Miller were already at work in the modern era; do you want to exclude e.g. Graham & Dodd from asset pricing?).  I'd cut "for many decades": for as long as there have been assets and markets, people have been trying to price them.

1. further _developing main arguments_:
    1. justification of Algorithm 1.  Yes, of course, we _can_ do this: why should we?  What properties does the algorithm have?  Is it 'greedy' in its addition of features?  If so, can anything be said about what sorts of datasets this is problematic for?
    1. relationship to existing uses of Shapley's value for model/feature selection (q.v. Lipovetsky & Conklin, 2001; Sundararajan & Najmi, 2020)?
    1. relationship to Agarwal et al.'s _neural additive models_ (q.v. https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.13912), which also seeks to maintain both accuracy and interpretability.  Would it be an appropriate benchmark for comparison?
    1. relationship to dropout: Shapley drops out features; the dropout parameter (p.6, CTR data) drops out hidden nodes.
    1. is there any advantage in using interaction indices/measures of joint feature importance, given the paper's interest in assessing feature interactions?
    1. the CTR 70:20:10 training:validation:test split seems unusual to me.  To what extent do the results depend on this?
    1. I'd like to see runtimes/compute costs in Tables 2 and 3.  I'd also like to see the models learned by the various asset pricing approaches: as the FFM5 has few features, I would expect that we should be able to gain intuitions from this exercise 

(Properly addressing these issues seems more fundamental to me than, say, improving the existing algorithm's approximation techniques.)
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper presents an approach for addressing model/feature selection in a performant and interpretable way - which is clearly an important goal.

At present, though, it presents very little theoretical defense of its approach (including by comparison to the existing literature), relying instead on a couple of examples.

By cutting extraneous material (e.g. all the 'data-centric' material), the main arguments can be buttressed to better convince the reader of the approach's validity.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to reviewer 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive and detailed comments. Please refer to the following for our response:

a)	“the manuscript burns space discussing 'data-centric methods'. In my view, this is a distraction that adds nothing to the main arguments, while cutting down on the space available to properly substantiate those arguments. I recommend cutting this material and bolstering the main arguments; there are minor typos and grammatical errors at a few places. In most cases, the authors' intent is intelligible, but it would be nice to clear them up; I'd re-draft the abstract to make it a bit clearer”

We agree with the reviewer that discussing data-centric methods may distract readers from the main exposition of the article. We will remove this part and bolster the main arguments of this work, including discussing the relationships with more related works, clarifying the unique properties of this method, and conducting more experiments to fully explore the properties of the method.  

b)	“\citep{} should be used in many of the cases that \cite{} or \citet{} is currently used; no footnotes in abstracts, by historical convention; the figures are too small to read.”

We will carefully re-check the manuscript to improve some imprecise expressions and increase the size of the image.

c)	“what's the difference between Ghorbani & Zou's 2019 application of Shapley to "each data sample" and "local Shapley values" (in the sense of Lundberg & Lee)?”

“Local Shapley values” are estimated to explain how a single feature affect the performance of a model. In the sense of Data Shapley, Ghorbani et.al. treat data samples as features. This enables to evaluate the contribution of each data sample to the model performance. 

d)	“I missed how the "toy" MovieLens analysis in \S 4.6 differed from the MovieLens analysis performed earlier in the manuscript. Thus, I'd recommend clarifying that paragraph.

Thank you for pointing out this problem. The Table 2 only presents the performance of the “new feature set” (i.e., the original features and feature interactions discovered by our method) evaluated by a linear regression model. Meanwhile, the toy test presented in section 4.6 aims to investigate whether the feature interaction discovered by our Feature Shapley is the optimal set of feature interaction. We hence enumerate all possible feature sets for the MovieLens dataset and visualize their performance evaluated by a linear regression model respectively. This verifies that the feature interactions discovered by our method is exactly the optimal feature set for the MovieLens dataset. We will clarify this subsection clearer.

content.title: Response to reviewer 1 (Part B)
content.comment:
e)	”justification of Algorithm 1. Yes, of course, we can do this: why should we? What properties does the algorithm have? Is it 'greedy' in its addition of features? If so, can anything be said about what sorts of datasets this is problematic for?”

Thank you for your suggestion. Our method benefits from the unique properties of Shapley value (e.g., symmetry, additivity, and ability to detect dummy player).
We will link these propertied to our work and justify the advantages of our method in the updated manuscript.

f)	“Relationship to existing uses of Shapley's value for model/feature selection (q.v. Lipovetsky & Conklin, 2001; Sundararajan & Najmi, 2020)? Relationship to Agarwal et al.'s neural additive models  (q.v. https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.13912), which also seeks to maintain both accuracy and interpretability. Would it be an appropriate benchmark for comparison? Relationship to dropout: Shapley drops out features; the dropout parameter (p.6, CTR data) drops out hidden nodes. Is there any advantage in using interaction indices/measures of joint feature importance, given the paper's interest in assessing feature interactions?”

Thank you for your suggestion. We will discuss these works in the updated manuscript.

g)	“the CTR 70:20:10 training:validation:test split seems unusual to me. To what extent do the results depend on this? ”

Thank you for raising this concern. In this work, we follow the setting presented in the existing works for a fair comparison. Although AFN indicates that the ratio of splitting is 8:1:1 in their paper. We found the splitting ratio of dataset downloaded from their repository (https://github.com/WeiyuCheng/AFN-AAAI-20) is 7:2:1. W found that only by using this ratio, can the results presented in their paper be reproduced. Hence, we followed their setting and presented the exact splitting ratio in this work.

h)	“I'd like to see runtimes/compute costs in Tables 2 and 3. I'd also like to see the models learned by the various asset pricing approaches: as the FFM5 has few features, I would expect that we should be able to gain intuitions from this exercise”

Indeed, the running time and compute cost should be presented. We are conducting related experiments, including computing the training time, inference time and number of parameters of all methods. We also agree with the reviewer that more experiments should be conducted for asset pricing scenarios as FFM5 only have 5 features. Therefore, we are running the following experiments: 1) add a comparing method that uses multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to implicitly learn feature interactions on the asset pricing dataset.  2) compare the Feature Shapley value computed by our method with the exact Shapley value on the asset pricing dataset.
